title: Sensitivity tables: which number moves the deal
summary: A sensitivity table recomputes one result, such as yield on cost or profit, while you change one or two inputs at a time. It shows which assumption the deal depends on most, and how far it can move before the deal stops working.
body:
A pro forma gives one answer; a sensitivity table gives the range of answers you might actually get. Change one or two inputs at a time, recompute, and look for the cell where the deal stops working.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, every pro forma is built on guesses: rents, costs, interest rates, cap rates, time. The single number at the bottom looks precise, but it is only as good as the guesses. A sensitivity table asks: if this guess is wrong by a sensible amount, what happens to the answer?

The method is mechanical:

  1. Pick the output you care about, such as yield on cost, profit or value.
  2. Pick one or two inputs you are least sure of.
  3. Move each input by a realistic step, for example 10 percent either way, and recompute the output for every combination.
  4. Find the breakeven: the input value at which the output hits your hurdle.

The formulas are the ones you already know from week one:

Yield on cost (percent) = stabilized NOI (dollars a year) ÷ total development cost (dollars) × 100

Value (dollars) = NOI (dollars a year) ÷ cap rate (as a decimal)

A worked example

A hypothetical project costs 20 million dollars and the pro forma shows stabilized NOI of 1.3 million dollars a year. Yield on cost = 1.3 ÷ 20 = 6.5 percent. Similar finished buildings trade at about a 5.5 percent cap rate, so the development spread is 1.0 percentage point.

Now test it. Let NOI move 10 percent either way, to 1.17 million or 1.43 million, and let cost either hold at 20 million or overrun by 10 percent to 22 million.

Stabilized NOICost 20 millionCost 22 million
1.17 million5.85 percent5.32 percent
1.30 million6.50 percent5.91 percent
1.43 million7.15 percent6.50 percent

Each cell is just NOI divided by cost. For example, the bottom-left cell is 1.17 ÷ 20 = 5.85 percent, and the cell in the middle of the right column is 1.30 ÷ 22 = 5.91 percent.

What does the table tell you?

  • A 10 percent miss on rent and a 10 percent cost overrun hurt about equally: each takes roughly 0.6 of a point off the yield.
  • With both at once, the yield falls to 5.32 percent, below the 5.5 percent cap rate. The spread is gone: you would have spent 22 million dollars building something you could have bought finished for less.
  • A 10 percent rent beat exactly cancels a 10 percent cost overrun: both corners on that diagonal show 6.5 percent.

Two habits make sensitivity tables honest. First, use realistic steps, based on how much that input has actually moved in past deals, not tiny steps chosen to make the table look calm. Second, remember the inputs are linked: in a weak market, rents soften, lease-up slows and cap rates rise together, so the bad corner of the table is more likely than it looks.

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

Problem 1

A project costs 10 million dollars with stabilized NOI of 700 thousand dollars. Find the yield on cost in the base case, with NOI down 10 percent, with cost up 10 percent, and with both.

Problem 2

A finished project will earn NOI of 1 million dollars a year and costs 17 million dollars to build. Work out value and profit at cap rates of 5, 5.5 and 6 percent. At what cap rate does profit hit zero?

Problem 3

You show a lender your sensitivity table. What would a lender ask about it?

The roommate question

In planning studies you vary load and generation dispatch to see which line overloads first. How is that like a sensitivity table, and what is the grid's equivalent of the "breakeven" cell?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
• Base: 700 ÷ 10,000 thousand = 7.0 percent.
  • NOI down 10 percent: 630 thousand ÷ 10 million = 6.3 percent.
  • Cost up 10 percent: 700 thousand ÷ 11 million = about 6.36 percent.
  • Both: 630 thousand ÷ 11 million = about 5.73 percent.

Notice that the NOI miss hurts slightly more than the cost overrun of the same size: cutting the top of the fraction by 10 percent cuts the yield by 10 percent, while raising the bottom by 10 percent cuts it by only about 9 percent.

The usual error: subtracting percentages, for example saying "7 minus 10 percent minus 10 percent equals 5 percent". Recompute the ratio each time.

Rule: recompute every cell from the inputs; never adjust the answer by hand.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
• 5 percent cap: value = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 million; profit = 20 − 17 = 3 million.
  • 5.5 percent cap: value = 1 ÷ 0.055 = about 18.18 million; profit about 1.18 million.
  • 6 percent cap: value = 1 ÷ 0.06 = about 16.67 million; profit about minus 0.33 million, a loss.
  • Breakeven cap rate: the cap rate at which value equals cost, so 1 million ÷ 17 million = about 5.88 percent. That is also the yield on cost.

A one-point move in the cap rate, which can happen over a construction period, swings profit by about 3.3 million dollars.

The usual error: treating the exit cap rate as fixed. It is a market guess set years before the sale, and value is very sensitive to it.

Rule: the breakeven exit cap rate equals your yield on cost.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• Why these step sizes? Are 10 percent moves realistic, or have rents and costs moved more than that in recent years?
  • What did you leave out? Interest rates, lease-up time and the exit cap rate all matter, not only rent and cost.
  • What happens to my coverage? A lender cares about debt service coverage in the bad cells, not only about your profit.
  • Who covers the bad corner? If both shocks happen, does more equity come in, and is there a guarantee?

The usual error: building a table only around the equity's profit. A lender reads the same table and looks for the cell where it stops being paid.

Rule: show the corner where the deal breaks, not just the middle where it works.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
A planning study varies conditions and recomputes flows to see which element limits the system and at what level. A sensitivity table does the same for a deal: it varies rent, cost or cap rate and recomputes the yield or profit. The grid's "breakeven cell" is the operating point where a line reaches its rating; the deal's is the input value at which yield falls to the cap rate or profit reaches zero. In both, the useful output is the margin to that limit, not the base-case number.

Rule: know the margin to the limit, not just today's value.

rule: Vary the inputs you trust least by realistic amounts, recompute every cell, and find the breakeven before you trust the base case.

title: Downside cases and the 1.20x DSCR breakpoint
summary: Debt service coverage ratio compares the income a building earns with the loan payments it must make. Lenders commonly size loans so coverage stays at or above about 1.20x, and the breakpoint tells you how far income or rates can move before you breach that line.
body:
The debt service coverage ratio, or DSCR, is income divided by loan payments, and lenders commonly want it at or above about 1.20 times. Work backwards from that line and you get the breakpoint: the lowest NOI, or the highest interest rate, the deal can survive.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, a construction loan is usually repaid by a permanent loan once the building is leased, and that permanent lender sizes its loan on coverage. The question it asks is: in a normal year, how many times over does the building's income pay the loan?

DSCR (times) = NOI (dollars a year) ÷ annual debt service (dollars a year)

Annual debt service is all the loan payments in a year: interest, and principal if the loan amortizes. To keep the arithmetic clean this week, we use interest-only loans, where:

Annual debt service (dollars) = loan amount (dollars) × interest rate (as a decimal)

A DSCR of 1.20x means the building earns 1.20 dollars for every 1 dollar of debt service, a 20 percent cushion. Many lenders use a minimum around 1.20x to 1.25x for apartments, often higher for riskier property types. That is common lender practice, not law, and the exact figure is negotiated loan by loan.

Rearrange the formula and you get the two breakpoints that matter:

Breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × annual debt service

Maximum debt service = NOI ÷ 1.20

A worked example

A hypothetical building earns stabilized NOI of 1.2 million dollars a year. The permanent loan is 15 million dollars, interest-only at 6 percent.

  1. Debt service = 15 million × 0.06 = 900 thousand dollars a year.
  2. DSCR = 1.2 million ÷ 900 thousand = 1.33x. Comfortably above 1.20x.
  3. Breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 900 thousand = 1.08 million dollars. NOI can fall by 120 thousand, which is 10 percent, before the deal breaches the line.
  4. Rate breakpoint: maximum debt service = 1.2 million ÷ 1.20 = 1 million dollars a year. On a 15 million dollar loan, that is a rate of 1 ÷ 15 = about 6.67 percent. A rise of about two thirds of a point breaches the line.
  5. Sizing: if the lender insists on 1.20x at 6 percent, the most it will lend is 1 million ÷ 0.06 = about 16.67 million dollars.

Building a downside case

A downside case is a single, coherent bad story, not a random cell. For example: "rents come in 5 percent low, vacancy runs 3 points higher, and operating costs rise 5 percent." Work each change through to NOI, then to DSCR, and compare with 1.20x. If the downside case breaches, you need a plan: a smaller loan, an interest-rate cap, a cash reserve, or more equity.

Why does breaching matter? Breaching a coverage covenant can trigger a cash sweep, where all spare cash goes to the lender, or a default. And if you were relying on a refinance to repay the construction loan, a smaller permanent loan leaves a gap that someone has to fill with cash.

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

All loans are interest-only. Use 1.20x as the minimum coverage.

Problem 1

NOI is 2 million dollars a year and annual debt service is 1.5 million dollars. What is the DSCR? What is the breakpoint NOI, and by what percentage can NOI fall before it is reached?

Problem 2

A 15 million dollar loan at 6 percent, with NOI of 1.25 million dollars. Find the DSCR. Then test two downside cases separately: NOI falls 15 percent; and the floating rate rises to 7 percent. Which breach 1.20x? What is the highest rate the deal can take at the base NOI?

Problem 3

Your downside case breaches 1.20x. What would a lender ask, and what are your options?

The roommate question

On the grid you keep a margin between the flow on a line and its rating. How is the 20 percent cushion in a 1.20x DSCR like an operating margin, and why is it not the same as the line's absolute limit?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. DSCR = 2 ÷ 1.5 = about 1.33x.
  2. Breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 1.5 million = 1.8 million dollars.
  3. Allowed fall = 2 − 1.8 = 0.2 million, and 0.2 ÷ 2 = 10 percent.

The usual error: thinking that a 1.33x ratio means NOI can fall 33 percent. It can only fall to the 1.20x line, so the room is 1 − 1.20 ÷ 1.33, about 10 percent.

Rule: room to fall = 1 − (1.20 ÷ current DSCR).

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Debt service = 15 million × 0.06 = 900 thousand. DSCR = 1.25 million ÷ 900 thousand = about 1.39x.
  2. NOI down 15 percent: 1.25 million × 0.85 = 1.0625 million. DSCR = 1.0625 ÷ 0.9 = about 1.18x. Breaches.
  3. Rate to 7 percent: debt service = 15 million × 0.07 = 1.05 million. DSCR = 1.25 ÷ 1.05 = about 1.19x. Breaches.
  4. Highest rate: maximum debt service = 1.25 million ÷ 1.20 = about 1.042 million. Rate = 1.042 ÷ 15 = about 6.94 percent.

A coverage of 1.39x looked comfortable, yet each of two quite ordinary shocks breaches it on its own.

The usual error: testing only income and forgetting the interest rate on floating-rate debt. The rate moves the denominator, which can be just as dangerous.

Rule: stress both the top of the ratio and the bottom.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
Lender questions:

  • How likely is the downside? What evidence supports your rents and your rate assumption?
  • Is the rate hedged? Will you buy an interest-rate cap, and at what strike?
  • What reserves exist? Is there an interest or operating reserve funded up front?
  • Who stands behind it? Is there a guarantee or a commitment to put in more equity to pay down the loan?

Options: borrow less so that coverage holds in the downside; fix or cap the rate; fund a reserve; or accept a cash sweep that pays the loan down from spare cash. Each costs the equity something, and that is the trade.

The usual error: treating a breach in the downside case as a reason to drop the downside case. The lender will run it anyway.

Rule: fix a downside breach with structure before closing, not hope after it.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
A line is not operated at its full rating; you hold a margin so that a contingency or a load swing does not push it over. A 1.20x DSCR is the lender's operating margin: the building is expected to earn 20 percent more than the loan needs, so a bad year does not stop payments. It is not the absolute limit, which is 1.00x, where income only just pays the loan and any further drop means a shortfall. Running at 1.05x is like running a line at 95 percent of its rating: legal for the moment, but with no room for the next event.

Rule: 1.20x is the operating margin; 1.00x is the cliff.

rule: DSCR is NOI divided by debt service; the 1.20x line common in lending gives you a breakpoint NOI of 1.20 times debt service, so stress both income and the rate against it.

title: Combined shocks and the pre-mortem
summary: Real downturns rarely arrive one variable at a time, so test income and interest rates together and find the breakpoints for each. A pre-mortem imagines the deal has already failed and works backwards to the causes, turning vague worries into numbers you can test.
body:
Shocks travel together, so the honest test combines them. A pre-mortem starts from "it failed" and asks why, which turns hidden worries into specific numbers you can check against the DSCR line.

The idea

Mr Shabazz, yesterday you tested one shock at a time. In a real downturn, rents soften, lease-up slows and interest rates rise in the same season, because they share a cause. A deal that survives each shock alone can fail when two arrive together.

The tool for finding those combinations is the pre-mortem. Before committing, the team imagines it is two years later and the project has failed. Each person writes down the most likely reason. Because the failure is treated as a fact, people name risks they would otherwise keep quiet about. Then you turn each reason into a number and test it.

A typical pre-mortem list for a rental development might read:

  • Construction ran 4 months late, so interest carry overran.
  • A competing building opened nearby and rents came in lower than planned.
  • The floating interest rate rose before the permanent loan was in place.
  • The permanent loan was sized smaller than expected, leaving a gap at refinance.

Each line becomes an input change: carry up by a known amount, NOI down by a percentage, rate up by a number of points. Then you run them together.

The formulas are the same as yesterday, with interest-only debt to keep it clean:

Debt service = loan × rate; DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service; breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × debt service

Remember that 1.20x is a common lender minimum, not a legal requirement.

A worked example

A hypothetical project has stabilized NOI of 1.3 million dollars and a 13 million dollar loan, interest-only at 6.5 percent.

  1. Base debt service = 13 million × 0.065 = 845 thousand. DSCR = 1.3 ÷ 0.845 = about 1.54x. Healthy.
  2. Pre-mortem shock one, rents miss so NOI falls 12 percent: NOI = 1.3 × 0.88 = 1.144 million. DSCR = 1.144 ÷ 0.845 = about 1.35x. Still fine.
  3. Pre-mortem shock two, the rate rises to 7.5 percent: debt service = 13 million × 0.075 = 975 thousand. At base NOI, DSCR = 1.3 ÷ 0.975 = about 1.33x. Still fine.
  4. Both together: DSCR = 1.144 ÷ 0.975 = about 1.17x. Below 1.20x.

Each shock alone left plenty of room; together they breach. Now find the breakpoints, which tell you how much room each risk really has:

  • At 6.5 percent, breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 845 thousand = 1.014 million, so NOI can fall 286 thousand, which is 22 percent.
  • At 7.5 percent, breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 975 thousand = 1.17 million, so NOI can fall only 130 thousand, which is 10 percent.

The rate rise did not breach the line by itself, but it cut the income cushion from 22 percent to 10 percent. That is the real finding of the pre-mortem: one risk quietly spends the margin that protects you from another.

The answer is rarely "do not build". It is usually structure: a rate cap, a slightly smaller loan, a funded reserve, or a fixed-price construction contract. Each one closes a specific line on the pre-mortem list.

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice.

Tonight's drill

All loans are interest-only, with 1.20x as the minimum coverage.

Problem 1

NOI is 900 thousand dollars and the loan is 10 million dollars at 6 percent. Find the DSCR, the breakpoint NOI and the percentage NOI can fall. Then find the highest interest rate the deal can take at the base NOI.

Problem 2

Same deal. Build a two-by-two table of DSCR with NOI of 900 thousand or 765 thousand (a 15 percent miss), and a rate of 6 or 7.5 percent. Which cells pass, which fail, and which one is a trap?

Problem 3

Run a short pre-mortem on this deal: name three reasons it might fail and, for each, what a lender would ask and what structure would answer it.

The roommate question

The grid is planned to survive the loss of any single element, the N-1 criterion. How is that different from a stress test that combines shocks, and which one is a pre-mortem closer to?

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Debt service = 10 million × 0.06 = 600 thousand. DSCR = 900 ÷ 600 = 1.50x.
  2. Breakpoint NOI = 1.20 × 600 thousand = 720 thousand dollars.
  3. Allowed fall = 180 thousand, and 180 ÷ 900 = 20 percent. Check: 1 − 1.20 ÷ 1.50 = 0.20.
  4. Maximum debt service = 900 thousand ÷ 1.20 = 750 thousand. Rate = 750 thousand ÷ 10 million = 7.5 percent.

The usual error: dividing the breakpoint by the wrong base. The percentage fall is measured against today's NOI, not against the breakpoint.

Rule: breakpoint NOI is 1.20 times debt service; maximum debt service is NOI divided by 1.20.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
Debt service is 600 thousand at 6 percent and 750 thousand at 7.5 percent.

NOI6 percent7.5 percent
900 thousand1.50x, pass1.20x, exactly on the line
765 thousandabout 1.28x, pass1.02x, fail

Workings: 900 ÷ 600 = 1.50; 900 ÷ 750 = 1.20; 765 ÷ 600 = 1.275; 765 ÷ 750 = 1.02.

The trap is the top-right cell. It passes only if the covenant says "at least 1.20x", and any further wobble breaches it. Treat a result sitting exactly on the line as a fail for planning purposes. The bottom-right cell is nearly at 1.00x: the building barely covers its interest.

The usual error: reporting each shock alone, both of which pass, and missing that together they almost wipe out coverage.

Rule: a result exactly on the line is not a margin.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
One good answer, among many:

  • Rates rise before the permanent loan. Lender asks: is the rate capped, and at what level? Structure: buy a rate cap at or below 7.5 percent, the breakpoint you found.
  • Rents miss because of new supply. Lender asks: what competing projects are planned nearby, and what are their rents? Structure: borrow less, or fund an interest reserve that covers the lease-up gap.
  • Construction runs late. Lender asks: is the contract fixed-price, and is there a completion guarantee? Structure: a fixed-price contract, a contingency, and enough interest reserve to cover several extra months.

The usual error: writing vague risks such as "the market turns". A pre-mortem item is only useful once it becomes a number you can test and a structure that answers it.

Rule: every pre-mortem reason should end as a number and a fix.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
N-1 planning makes sure the system survives the loss of any one element. A combined stress test asks what happens when several things go wrong at once, which on the grid is closer to N-1-1 or an extreme-event study. The lesson is the same in both fields: correlated failures are where systems that passed every single-contingency test still go down. A pre-mortem is closer to the extreme-event study, because it starts from an outcome and asks which combination of causes would produce it.

Rule: passing every single shock does not mean you survive two at once.

rule: Test shocks together, find the breakpoint for each, and use a pre-mortem to turn every way the deal could fail into a number and a fix.
